What counts as a slot or a finish window?

A slot is one unit of space you have measured in your oven. A large pan might need two slots. Check rack clearance and airflow yourself. Matching temperatures alone do not make dishes suitable to cook together.

“Finish before serving” is the time between leaving the oven and dinner. Minimum includes your recipe’s required rest or cooling time; maximum is the earliest you want the dish done. For an exact finish, enter the same number twice. These are scheduling preferences, not safe holding limits.

THE SAMPLE PLAN

Your timeline

A schedule is not a food-safety check.

Use tested recipes and a food thermometer. This tool does not verify doneness, reheating, cooling or safe holding. A long finish window does not make food safe to leave out. Read USDA’s Thanksgiving safety guidance before planning your meal.

THE METHOD

Work backward.
Keep the constraints.

  1. Copy, don’t estimate.

    Take each oven temperature and duration from your own recipe. Include a realistic heat-change buffer for your oven.

  2. Give each dish a window.

    Enter its required rest and the earliest it may finish. If you need a specific end time, make both values equal.

  3. Read the result honestly.

    A matching plan fits the numbers. A clash needs a changed input or menu. A search-limit result is inconclusive.

What this checker can’t know

It models one oven, one fixed temperature per dish, measured pan slots and whole-minute timing. It allows overlapping dishes only at exactly equal entered temperatures. It does not model prep, burners, multiple cooking stages, loading time, rack-specific heat, convection changes, thermal recovery or safe food holding. Buffer minutes are your estimate, not an oven measurement. Check the plan against your recipes and equipment.

Changing only the serve time shifts the schedule; it won’t resolve a relative oven conflict. See the one-oven planning guide for a worked example and ways to rethink a clash.
